t: LeetCode 1676 — Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree IV: One Post-Order Target Count
o:
Given a binary tree with unique values and an array of k distinct nodes that all exist in the tree, return the deepest node that has every listed node as a descendant, where a node counts as its own descendant.

Example 1 asks for LCA(4, 7) = 2; Example 2 shows a singleton list returns the node itself (LCA(1) = 1); Example 3 asks for LCA(7, 6, 2, 4) = 5 - deeper than the root because all four targets live under node 5.

With up to 10^4 nodes we want one O(n) traversal rather than k separate searches, and uniqueness of values lets us identify targets by reference or by value in a hash set.
k: The multi-node LCA is simply the deepest node whose subtree contains all k targets.
One post-order pass counting matched targets per subtree finds it: the first node in bottom-up order whose count reaches k is the answer.
Reusing the classic two-node LCA k-1 times also works, at O(k*n) instead of O(n).

a.n: Approach 1: Fold the Pairwise LCA Across the Array
a.i: LCA(p1..pk) equals LCA(...LCA(LCA(p1,p2),p3)...). Run the textbook two-node recursion k-1 times, carrying the running answer forward. Simple to reason about because each step is the well-known LC 236 subroutine.
s: For each subsequent node x, compute lca(root, ans, x): a null node or a node matching either target returns itself.
Combine child results: both non-null means the current node is their split point.
Assign each result back to ans and continue through the array.
a.t: O(k*n) — each fold may traverse the entire tree
a.sp: O(h) — recursion stack, h the tree height

a.i: During one post-order DFS, return for each node how many targets live in its subtree (itself included). The first node whose count hits k is the lowest common ancestor - deeper candidates appear earlier in post-order, so recording only the first hit is correct. Targets go into a hash set keyed by node reference (or by value, since values are unique).
s: Insert all k targets into a hash set.
DFS children first; each node returns leftCount + rightCount + (itself being a target).
When a node count equals k and no answer has been recorded yet, store that node.
Return the stored node after the traversal completes.
a.t: O(n) — every node is visited exactly once
a.sp: O(n) — hash set plus recursion stack up to tree height

w:
Present the counting DFS as your main solution: one pass, no repeated scans, and it generalizes verbatim to "deepest node containing this subset".
Edge cases worth calling out: a single-target list answers that node itself; targets stacked on one ancestor-descendant chain are handled naturally by counting (naive early-return pairwise shortcuts can miss these); skewed trees reach depth 10^4, so bump the Python recursion limit or iterate with an explicit stack.
Follow-ups: many queries on a static tree lead to binary lifting or Tarjan offline LCA; if targets might not exist, validate during the same DFS by checking the final count equals k.
